historical_timeline.summary: Operation for a uterine tumor, with a hysterectomy done without her knowledge or consent.
Tried to register to vote; evicted from the plantation the same night.
Arrested and beaten in the Winona jail; lifelong injuries to her eyes, legs and kidneys.
Testimony before the Credentials Committee in Atlantic City.
Final hospital admission in Mound Bayou for complications of heart disease, diabetes and breast cancer.

claims.statement: Fannie Lou Hamer was born on October 6, 1917, in Montgomery County, Mississippi, the twentieth child of Lou Ella and James Lee Townsend, sharecroppers. She joined her family in the cotton fields at six and left school after the sixth grade, at 12, to work on the cotton plantations of the Delta.

She worked for eighteen years as a sharecropper and timekeeper on a Delta plantation, made timekeeper because she could read and write. In 1964 she gave her home as Ruleville, in Sunflower County, Mississippi.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors her literacy, her rural Delta home and her work history in the modern social history.

source_links.locator: her testimony gives her address in Ruleville, Sunflower County, and eighteen years on the plantation

claims.statement: In 1961, hospitalized for abdominal pain, she was found to have a uterine tumor; during the operation to remove it, a white surgeon performed a hysterectomy without her knowledge or informed consent. She later called this a "Mississippi appendectomy," a name for the sterilizations done without consent to Black women in the South.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for the teaching contrast: in the modern episode every examination, test and procedure is explained in advance and done only with her documented consent, and her right to refuse is respected. Her mistrust of medical care was earned.

source_links.locator: she later called it her Mississippi appendectomy

claims.statement: On August 31, 1962, she tried to register to vote in Indianola; when she refused to withdraw her application, the plantation owner ordered her off his land and she had to leave that same night.

On June 9, 1963, returning from a voter-registration workshop, she was arrested with other activists in Winona, Mississippi, and in the jail two Black prisoners were ordered by officers to beat her with a blackjack, as she testified the next year.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors the history of injury and the trauma-informed approach in the modern episode.

claims.statement: The beating left her with lifelong injuries to her eyes, legs and kidneys: permanent kidney damage, and a blood clot in her left eye with loss of vision in one eye.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for the modern kidney history and the reduced vision in her left eye. The modern kidney findings are synthetic.

source_links.locator: lost vision in one eye and permanent kidney damage
kidney damage and a blood clot in her eye
a blood clot over her left eye and permanent damage to one of her kidneys

claims.statement: On August 22, 1964, she testified before the Credentials Committee of the Democratic National Convention in Atlantic City about her eviction and the Winona beating.

In her late fifties she found a lump in her left breast and did not seek care for it at first. Appeals were made to help with her mounting medical bills. In early 1977 she was admitted for the last time to the hospital in Mound Bayou, where she was treated for complications of heart disease, diabetes and breast cancer.
claims.clinical_interpretation: History after the modern episode. Anchors the later diabetes and the cost barriers in the modern record; the breast cancer appears only as history and in screening.

claims.statement: She died on March 14, 1977, in Mound Bayou, Mississippi, at 59. Accounts of the cause differ: complications of hypertension and breast cancer, complications of heart disease and cancer, or breast cancer.
claims.clinical_interpretation: History only, a decade after the modern episode. Anchors the later hypertension.

source_links.locator: complications of hypertension and breast cancer

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Hypertension, type 2 diabetes and kidney disease in a 49-year-old community organizer in the rural Mississippi Delta, managed at a community health center with trauma-informed care. The teaching contrast is her documented sterilization without consent: here every examination, test and procedure is explained beforehand, done only with her documented consent, with a chaperone of her choosing, and stopped or declined at her word without loss of care. The episode covers confirming hypertension with home readings under the 2025 AHA/ACC guideline, diagnosing and treating diabetes under the ADA Standards of Care 2026, kidney function and urine albumin with KDIGO, an ACE inhibitor and an SGLT2 inhibitor, a statin, retinal photographs, foot care, medication choices for cost and adherence, a community health worker on the team, a social needs screen with real resources for food, transportation and utility costs, shared decisions, and preventive care.

visit_schedule.purpose: Establishing care at the rural community health center for high blood pressure readings, thirst and frequent urination, leg and back aching, and reduced vision in the left eye since an old injury, with consent-based, trauma-informed care and a social needs screen
Two-week review of home blood pressure readings and the repeat urine test, with a kidney ultrasound and a nephrology telehealth consultation from the health center
Six-week review: blood pressure, kidney function and potassium after the new medicines, lipids, retinal photographs, and benefits
Four-month review: A1c, urine albumin, kidney function, mood, social needs, and the metformin dose
Seven-month review: A1c, urine albumin, kidney function, seasonal and age-50 vaccines, screening results, and plans for the winter

hpi.narrative: Mrs. Hamer returns two weeks after her first visit. She took her home blood pressure twice a day for seven days with the cuff the health center gave her, and the community health worker helped her write the readings down; they average 152/94. Her thirst and frequent urination are already less on metformin, with some loose stools in the first week that have settled. She had her kidney ultrasound this morning at the health center, after the sonographer explained each step; she asked for her companion to stay in the room, and she did. She then spoke with Dr. Agbaje of nephrology by video from the clinic, with the community health worker beside her. Her SNAP and energy assistance applications have been sent. She asked why she needs two new medicines and what they will cost.

referral.question: Albumin in the urine and mildly reduced kidney function in a 49-year-old woman with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure readings awaiting home confirmation, and kidneys injured in a beating years ago. Please advise on the cause, the need for imaging, kidney-protective treatment, and monitoring. A telehealth visit from our health center is requested, because the trip to the regional hospital is long and she has no car
referral.urgency: Within two weeks, by telehealth on the day of her two-week visit, with our community health worker present
referral.pertinent_history: She reports lasting kidney damage and reduced vision in her left eye since a beating in a jail years ago. Years before that, an operation for a uterine tumor included a hysterectomy done without her knowledge or consent; she is wary of medical care, wants every step explained, and decides what she agrees to; she agreed to this history being shared with you. Today she has had thirst and frequent urination for some months and aching legs and back. Blood pressure 164/98 (average of two readings), pulse 84, weight 93.0 kg, BMI 35.0. Results today: A1c 8.6%; random glucose 238 mg/dL; sodium 139, potassium 4.3 mmol/L; creatinine 0.96 mg/dL, eGFR 73 (CKD-EPI 2021); urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio 88 mg/g; total cholesterol 228, LDL 146, HDL 44, triglycerides 190 mg/dL; ALT 24, AST 22 U/L; hemoglobin 12.6 g/dL; platelets 268; TSH 2.1. ECG: sinus rhythm without left ventricular hypertrophy. Started today: metformin extended-release and atorvastatin 40 mg; a home blood pressure monitor for seven days; no NSAIDs. A repeat urine albumin test and a kidney ultrasound at the health center are planned for the morning of your visit, if she agrees. Social needs: food, transportation and utility costs; she has no health insurance and uses our sliding-fee scale and discount pharmacy
questions: What is the likely cause of the albuminuria and reduced eGFR: her old kidney injury, diabetes, high blood pressure, or a combination?
Is a kidney ultrasound needed, and does anything else need to be excluded?
If hypertension is confirmed, which blood pressure medicines do you advise, and what is her target?
Should she start an SGLT2 inhibitor now, and is there a role for finerenone?
Is metformin safe at this kidney function, and what should she avoid?
How often should kidney function, potassium and urine albumin be checked, given how hard travel is for her?

consultant_note.history: Mrs. Hamer, 49, is seen by video from the community health center at the request of Dr. Batiste-Hill, with the community health worker beside her and her consent to the telehealth visit. She describes injuries to her kidneys and left eye from a beating years ago, and back and leg aching since. She has had thirst and frequent urination for some months, easing on metformin. Her home blood pressure readings over seven days average 152/94. She takes no NSAIDs. She has no blood in the urine, no kidney stones and no known family kidney disease. She said she would agree to treatment if each medicine and its purpose were explained, and asked what the medicines would cost
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Dr. Batiste-Hill's intake note and results: creatinine 0.96 mg/dL, eGFR 73; potassium 4.3 mmol/L; urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio 88 mg/g at intake and 96 mg/g this morning; A1c 8.6%; LDL 146 mg/dL; ECG without left ventricular hypertrophy. Kidney ultrasound this morning: right kidney 9.0 cm with a lower-pole cortical scar, left kidney 11.4 cm and normal, no hydronephrosis or stones. Home blood pressure average 152/94; clinic 156/96 today

exam.finding: By video: comfortable and engaged, speaking in full sentences
Blood pressure 156/96 and pulse 82, measured by the clinic nurse today
No ankle swelling, as examined by Dr. Batiste-Hill today

assessment.assessment: The small, scarred right kidney is a structural abnormality consistent with her old injury and is in itself chronic kidney disease; with an eGFR of 73 and albuminuria confirmed on two samples, she is G2 A2. Diabetes and high blood pressure probably add to the albumin loss. Nothing on ultrasound suggests blockage, stones or another cause, and no further imaging is needed

Stage 2 hypertension is confirmed by home readings. With albuminuria an ACE inhibitor is the foundation, and at this level two medicines together are recommended; a single combined capsule keeps cost and pill count down. Target below 130/80

assessment.display: Type 2 diabetes with chronic kidney disease
assessment.assessment: An SGLT2 inhibitor protects the kidneys and heart at her eGFR and albuminuria, independent of its glucose effect. Metformin is safe at this eGFR at full dose. Finerenone is for albuminuria that persists despite an ACE inhibitor at the dose she tolerates and an SGLT2 inhibitor, and can wait

recommendations: Amlodipine 5 mg with benazepril 20 mg as one daily capsule; blood pressure goal below 130/80, with home readings
Dapagliflozin 10 mg daily, at the health center's discount pharmacy price; stop it, with benazepril, on days of vomiting, diarrhea or not eating, and restart when eating and drinking again
Potassium and creatinine one to two weeks after starting, accepting a creatinine rise of up to 30%; then every six months, scheduled on days she is already at the health center
Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio again in three to four months, then every six months; aim for at least a 30% fall
Continue metformin and atorvastatin; avoid ibuprofen, naproxen and other NSAIDs, and tell any clinician about her kidneys before contrast dye
No further imaging; repeat the ultrasound only if kidney function falls unexpectedly
If albumin stays moderately increased after six months on both medicines, review by telehealth about increasing benazepril or adding finerenone
